title: Two Addresses
synopsis: Pixel at seventeen, walking from East Pulse intake to a corner building with two real addresses. The landlord doesn't take her credits the first month — he takes a favor he'll name later. She moves into Unit 2E with one bag, names the workbench, and takes her first augment job in GLMZ from an old woman whose cardiac assist is misaligned.
html:
# Two Addresses

The building was exactly the way the woman on the bus had said it would be. Cream brick, rounded at the corner, two real addresses on the doorframe. Pixel — she was practicing the name, even in her head; *Pixel, Pixel* — stood across the intersection for a full minute before she crossed.

Not from fear. From wanting to remember.

She had been raised by a person who taught her that the moment before you walked into a place was a moment that belonged to you, and you could spend it however you wanted. *Spend it well,* her mother used to say, and what she meant was *don't rush past the door, the door is where you decide to be different.*

Pixel decided, on the corner of Ashland and Chicago, to become someone who lived in a building with two addresses. It was a small decision and it was instant and it stuck.

She crossed.

The Chicago Avenue door was the one that opened. The Ashland door was decorative — older, varnished, locked with a key she didn't have and might never have. The Chicago door had a standard cylinder lock and a button that connected to nothing visible and a hand-lettered card slipped behind a brass plate that read MR. ADAMU 2D, FOR INQUIRIES.

She knocked on the doorframe rather than pressing the button.

A voice from the second-floor window: "Up here."

Mr. Adamu was sixty, pear-shaped, with the careful tired eyes of someone who had outlived three different landlord eras and adjusted each time. He came down in slippers. He looked at her toolkit before he looked at her face. He said, "Auntie sent you," without ascertainment, and Pixel said, "Yes," and Mr. Adamu said, "Come up. Don't take the boots off, I don't care, the floor doesn't care, I will tell you who cares about the floor in a minute."

The unit was 2E. Across the hall from a closed door marked 2F that smelled, faintly, of clean motor oil and a kind of soap she didn't recognize.

"That's Mr. Corbin-Vasik," Mr. Adamu said, when he saw her notice the door. "He cares about the floor. Outside his unit. Inside his unit he doesn't care. Inside *yours* you can do whatever the building structurally permits, which is a very generous range."

The unit had: two windows, one over Chicago and one over the alley. A hot plate. A radiator from 2040 that he made her listen to before he agreed to the lease. A bathroom with a tub. A closet. A wall socket that he warned her not to overload but that she immediately knew she would overload, because *of course she would,* because she knew what she was going to do with the unit and the unit's wall socket did not yet know.

"Two-fifty Quanta a month," Mr. Adamu said. "You don't have it."

"Not yet."

"First month is a favor. You'll do something for me. I'll name it later. It will be reasonable."

"What's the favor going to be."

"I don't know yet," Mr. Adamu said, and the careful tired eyes glinted with something that was not quite humor and not quite warning. "That's the point. The favor is the thing I don't yet know I'll need. You'll be here when I need it."

"I'll be here."

"That's the contract."

She slept on the floor that night because she did not yet have a bed. The radiator from 2040 ran softly, the way a kettle that hasn't quite boiled runs softly, a working presence. Through the wall she could hear the building's electrical hum and somewhere — she did not know where, she would never quite locate it — a music she did not recognize, low, late, considered. She made a small inventory before sleep.

*One bag. One toolkit. The boots. The packet from Auntie. A unit. A landlord. A favor I owe and don't yet know.*

She slept. She did not dream of the cornfields. She dreamed of nothing she could remember, which she took, in the morning, as a kindness.

## ── ── ──

The workbench arrived on day three.

It was not bought. It was *constructed*, which was a different verb. She walked the alley behind the Pivot with the eyes of a person who had been pricing components since age nine and had a clear ranking system for materials her mother had taught her — *steel beats wood beats plastic,* her mother had said, *unless the plastic is the right plastic, in which case the plastic wins, but you will know.* On day three Pixel found a 1.6-meter slab of laminated steel bedrock, a stress fracture across one corner, in a contractor's discard pile behind a building that was being eaten by another building. She paid for it in attention — she stood next to the man dismantling the building until he noticed her, and she said *can I take that,* and the man, who had a son her age somewhere east, looked at the slab and looked at her and said *you carry that yourself, you can have it.*

She carried it herself. It took an hour. The freight elevator in The Pivot had been broken since 2197 and would remain broken until it killed someone, which in Mr. Adamu's calculation was a different problem. She brought the slab up the back stairs in three pieces — she had brought a saw, *of course* she had brought a saw — and reassembled it on the floor of Unit 2E with bolts and a steel band, and at hour four she had a workbench.

She named it *Maeve*. She did not know why. It just was Maeve.

"Hello, Maeve," she said, and the workbench did not say anything back, but Maeve was a thing that existed now, a thing she had made.

She stood in the unit, alone, with Maeve.

She thought, with the small clear surprise that was becoming her particular form of grace: *I am not, actually, doing this badly.*

## ── ── ──

The first patient was Mrs. Eldering on the first floor.

Mrs. Eldering was eighty, Czech-Trinidadian, retired-from-something-she-wouldn't-discuss, and her cardiac assist had been chirping on the wrong beat for four days and her grandson didn't know what to do and her grandson worked at the noodle shop on the next block where Mr. Adamu ate twice a week, and the chain of mention from the noodle shop to Mr. Adamu to Mrs. Eldering to *the new girl in 2E with the good toolkit* took seventeen minutes.

Pixel knocked on the door of 1A.

"It's me," she said, even though Mrs. Eldering had no idea who *me* was. "It's Pixel. Mr. Adamu sent me."

Mrs. Eldering opened the door. Mrs. Eldering looked at her with the assessing eye of a woman who had watched the GLMZ swallow specialists and unlicensed pretenders in equal proportion for sixty years.

"You're little," Mrs. Eldering said.

"I'm aware."

"Are you good."

"My mother was good. She taught me. So either yes or working on it."

Mrs. Eldering let her in.

The cardiac assist was a Bauer-Naidu unit, fifteen years out of warranty, the kind of thing licensed cyberdocs would tell you needed to be replaced. It did not need to be replaced. It needed to be cleaned and recalibrated and the contact at the third lead pad needed three minutes of patient attention with one of the brass-handled probes from the canvas roll. Pixel did the work in twenty-eight minutes. She narrated quietly while she worked because she had decided early — fourteen, kitchen table, watching her mother — that silence over someone's nervous system was a kind of disrespect. The patient deserved a voice. The voice did not need to be interesting. It needed to be *there.*

"There's a degraded contact on the third lead. Just gunk. I'm cleaning it. Hold still. I know — I know it tickles, that's the gel. The chirp is going to stop in about a minute. There. Hear it? That's the right interval. That's what you should have been hearing."

Mrs. Eldering listened.

Mrs. Eldering started to cry, the dry brief crying of a person who had stopped trusting the small mercies and had to relearn one in the moment.

"I haven't slept," Mrs. Eldering said. "In four days. The wrong rhythm gets in your sleep."

"You'll sleep tonight."

Mrs. Eldering paid her thirty Quanta and a jar of pickled cucumbers and a slip of paper that said *if anyone gives you trouble in this building tell them you are with me.*

Pixel walked back up the stairs to Unit 2E.

She set the thirty Quanta on Maeve. She set the cucumbers on Maeve. She unfolded the slip of paper and looked at Mrs. Eldering's signature — a *clean* signature, the practiced cursive of someone who had owned things — and put the paper in the canvas roll, snapped the roll closed.

She sat on the floor next to Maeve.

She thought, very carefully:

*I have a workbench. I have a patient who lived. I have thirty Quanta and a jar of cucumbers and a sentence I can carry into a fight if I need to.*

*I am here.*

*This is the unit. This is the floor. This is the wall.*

*This is the start of it.*

She turned the music on.

Low at first. Then, after a minute, *louder*, because she had decided that a person who had survived the bus and the cornfield and the corner of Ashland and Chicago, and had arrived alive in a unit with a workbench named Maeve, deserved music she could feel in her teeth.

The radiator from 2040 ran softly underneath. The wall socket did not yet know what was coming.

In 2F, across the hall, Mr. Corbin-Vasik — whoever he was — paused, briefly, behind his door. Pixel did not know about the pause.

She was busy. She was home.
